seasons.review_body: 1670 launched on Netflix December 13, 2023, as Poland's first Netflix mockumentary original and immediately became a cultural event: 11 weeks in Poland's domestic Top 10 and the Eagle Award from the Polish Film Academy for Best TV Series. Created by Jakub Ruzylllo, the eight-episode season deploys the Office-style talking-head format to satirise the 17th-century szlachta nobility while clearly targeting contemporary Polish social attitudes. Polish critics were enthusiastic - Radio Eska called it a masterpiece, and the Filmweb audience score reached 8.0. International Western reception was more divided: Decider's Joel Keller found the satire over-the-top and unfocused in the opening episode; the Rotten Tomatoes sample of two critics landed at 95 percent. The IMDb rating of 8.0 positions it among the better-received Netflix European comedies.

The series establishes its satirical register quickly - the 17th century setting is a costume for very contemporary Polish attitudes toward hierarchy and ambition.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# 1670 S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Jan Paweł Adamczewski begins with time itself. The year is 1670, time flies, and he says it as if history has been waiting for his commentary. Then the frame moves to starving peasant children, Marek, Józia, and Darek. That cut is the pilot's argument in miniature. **Jan Paweł** speaks in the language of national greatness while the world around him keeps presenting unpaid bills, hungry bodies, unread letters, and procedures sharp enough to gut a plan in two words. The premiere works because it makes delusion practical. The joke is not that Jan Paweł dreams too big. Every institution around him is somehow worse.

## Grandeur Arrives With Hungry Children

The opening minutes build Jan Paweł as a man addicted to scale. He jokes about 1670 and the speed of time, then points out starving peasant children as if misery is a detail in his personal tour. That is a sharp pilot move because it establishes a comic ruler before it establishes a plot. The episode does not need Jan Paweł to be smart. It needs him to be certain.

His stated aim is immense: absolute prosperity for Poland. The size matters. A smaller wish would make him a local fool. This one makes him a national fool, a man who treats public suffering as set dressing for private mythology. The prayer scene sharpens the contradiction. He tries to maintain his prosperity-for-Poland posture while interruptions keep breaking the pose. The piety is sincere enough to be dangerous and vain enough to be ridiculous.

The pilot also shows restraint in staging hypocrisy. It does not need a speech explaining that Jan Paweł sees peasants as props. It lets him gesture toward Marek, Józia, and Darek, then keeps moving. The children are specific, named, present. His rhetoric is huge and useless. The gap between those scales becomes the engine of the episode.

## The Letter Becomes a Leadership Test

The assembly letter turns incompetence into performance. Jan Paweł reads it aloud by watching and leading the peasants, a detail that says plenty without pausing for explanation. He wants authority, yet his authority depends on cues from the people under him. Literacy, status, and showmanship collide in one small public act.

That is the pilot's cleanest comic mechanism: power keeps needing help from below, then pretending the help never happened. Jan Paweł's later claim at the family assembly-meeting that he deciphered the encrypted message continues the bit. The message leads to the territorial assembly, but he frames the path there as proof of his own superior capacity. A simpler version would stop at his shaky reading. This version goes after reputation. He cares less about understanding the message than owning the story of how it was understood.

"Encrypted" does useful work. It inflates a practical invitation into something grander and more conspiratorial, which fits Jan Paweł's self-image. The episode keeps turning ordinary governance into heroic theatre, then punctures the theatre with timing. A letter is just a letter. In Jan Paweł's house, it becomes a legend about Jan Paweł.

## Maciej Is the Useful Counterweight

**Maciej** brings a quieter kind of comedy. He wants to work, help with blacksmithing, and manage his new role. The detail that he feeds horses only after tasks are assigned gives him a different rhythm from Jan Paweł. He is not powered by grand declarations. He moves when the world gives him a job.

The contrast matters. If everyone played the same loud register, the pilot would become a costume sketch stretched past its strength. Maciej grounds the household side of the episode. His comedy comes from navigation rather than proclamation: how to be useful, when to act, what role to occupy. Around Jan Paweł, work becomes a story about status. Around Maciej, work remains work.

The premiere could use more shape around him. His beats establish function more than pressure. He helps, waits, responds, and adjusts, while the central argument belongs elsewhere. Still, his presence keeps the episode from becoming a parade of noble absurdity. The blacksmithing and horse-feeding details pull the comedy back to labor, the thing Jan Paweł's rhetoric keeps floating above.

Maciej's smallness on the plot board is not a flaw by itself. The pilot is setting a social machine in motion. He is one of the gears that does not announce itself as a gear.

## Cicero Meets the Veto

The nobility assembly gives the episode its proper comic set-piece. **Andrzej** wants higher taxes approved and tries to win the debate. His method matters: he reaches for classical rhetoric, invoking Cicero as part of the strategy. The choice is perfectly pitched for this world. The characters do not merely argue policy. They decorate policy with borrowed grandeur, as if a Latin shadow can carry a tax increase over the line.

Then procedure wins. The motion to raise taxes is denied through liberum veto, and the episode's grand machinery collapses with almost insulting efficiency. This is where the pilot's thesis clicks into place. Jan Paweł wants prosperity. Andrzej wants the tax plan. The nobility has ceremonial language, assembly structure, and room for debate. The result is paralysis.

That is a smart target for the first episode because it gives the comedy a system, not just a personality. Jan Paweł's vanity is funny, but the liberum veto makes the world itself comic. The institutions are not neutral containers for foolish people. They generate foolish outcomes with a straight face. The episode understands that a blocked vote can be a punchline if the build-up is pompous enough.

The slight weakness is that Andrzej's debate strategy, at least from the available beats, sounds more like a clean sketch than a fully escalating sequence. The Cicero move is funny in concept, and the veto pays it off, but the middle could use another turn of pressure to make the denial sting harder. As a pilot engine, though, it works. The show has found a procedural joke with teeth.

## The Peasant Gets the Last Accounting

The final payoff belongs to the peasants' side of the equation. A peasant reports being victorious at the assembly and will not pay higher taxes. That is the right closing angle. After an episode of noble self-importance, the consequence is announced from below, in language that stumbles toward triumph and lands on money.

The mangled route to "victorious" fits the pilot's comic politics. Nobody owns perfect language here. Jan Paweł mangles moral perspective. Andrzej hides a fiscal push inside rhetoric. The peasant trips over the word for winning, then understands the outcome with total clarity: no higher taxes. The gap between vocabulary and material interest is the joke, and the material interest wins.

This also plants the season's immediate pressure points. Andrzej's scheme has failed for now, the peasants' status has shifted because the assembly result gives them leverage, and the supposedly encrypted message still has unanswered content beyond the invitation. The pilot does not close with chaos for its own sake. It closes with a practical reversal. The people meant to be taxed leave with the cleanest victory.

That is the premiere's strongest instinct. It lets the powerful perform intelligence and lets the powerless understand the bill.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a sharp, sturdy pilot that finds its comic spine early: national ambition keeps crashing into petty procedure, social dependence, and basic hunger. Jan Paweł is already a strong center because his contradiction is simple and renewable. He wants prosperity for Poland, then backs a tax push that dies inside the noble machinery meant to authorize it. The hour is funniest when it lets institutions behave like jokes without winking at them: the letter, the family assembly-meeting, the Cicero flourish, the veto. It is thinner around Maciej and could give Andrzej's debate a harder middle beat, but the final peasant payoff proves the engine works. For the season, the premiere plants a clean conflict between noble fantasy and material consequence, with enough unanswered business to keep the machine turning.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp pilot where noble grandeur trips over procedure, hunger, and the peasants who understand the bill best.

bollymeter.basis: 81% on Rotten Tomatoes from 1 review; the show maintained domestic popularity and earned its Season 3 renewal before Season 2 released.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 arrived September 17, 2025, continuing Jan Pawel's village-level schemes with the same ensemble. The Rotten Tomatoes sample remains thin at one review and 81 percent. The show had already secured a Season 3 renewal by April 2025, reflecting Netflix's confidence in its domestic and international audience. Critical aggregate coverage of the second season remained minimal in English-language press; Polish reception tracked broadly consistent with the enthusiastic first-season response.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 retains the mockumentary format and the ensemble without a reported structural shift; the pre-production Season 3 greenlit confirms the series is in its stride.
